name: desktop
title: A house worth coming back to · Family gifting
mainText:
A private return visit · For NickA house worthcoming back to.The shopping dashboard is really a family gifting table: remember what people love, gather ideas, plan celebrations and know who is buying what.The findingBuilt rooms.A broken front door.There is substantial app here. A fresh local setup reaches the sign-in screen, then fails. Keep the useful foundations; reconsider the living space.
Thoughtful gifts. Shared responsibility. Less to remember.Built in codeFamily memoryPeople, preferences, occasions, gifts and budgets.Built in codePlanning tableLinked lists, buying stages, comments and quick actions.Blocked in this visitFront doorA fake account can be created. Signing into it fails.Mostly on paperUpstairsPhone capture, richer sharing, deal watching and smart suggestions.A private household home, with a browser front and a shared store of family memory.
Where it stoppedHoliday polish,then a long pause.The last holiday feature work improved selecting gifts and acting on them together. Before that came richer recipient profiles, linked gifts, budgets, pictures and faster card actions. Most of the later phone redesign remained unfinished.There was maintenance this autumn, including changes to app code. The record does not explain why product work paused. Some progress sheets still contradict the code, so their completion labels cannot settle what works.
What exists todayThe lights come on.The door stays shut.The database and service started locally, and the browser rendered real pages. Creating a clearly fake account succeeded. Signing in failed because a later database update removes the change-history table that sign-in still tries to read.That blocks today’s check of gifts, lists and budgets. Their implementation exists; their complete household workflows were not proven on this visit.These are fresh captures of the running app.The family’s existing database was never opened. No family records were sent elsewhere. External fonts were blocked, which makes some icons appear as words.The broken front doorThe browser shows a fetch error. A direct service request identifies the missing database table underneath it.The account form rendersAccount creation worked through the service. Automatic sign-in is still blocked; this image alone proves the form renders.The house has furnishingsThe existing component gallery runs. It shows the current visual ingredients, not an authenticated family dashboard.
What was imaginedRooms stilldrawn in pencil.Historical ideas, not a new roadmap.Idea onlyA family inspiration roomFreeform boards and occasion moodboards. The narrower buying-stage board already exists in code.Idea onlyA thoughtful buying assistantPrice watching, deal alerts and personalized suggestions. A separate inspiration prototype tried suggestions; the actual app does not integrate them.Idea onlyDoors from other placesPhone sharing, browser capture, calendar connections, Apple sign-in and invitations that reveal only the right gifts.Partly builtA comfortable phone homeBasic phone layout and home-screen support exist. Gestures, dependable offline use and push reminders were left unfinished. No native phone app exists.
Where the gaps areSome doors leadto empty rooms.Coordination is incomplete“My Assignments” deliberately returns an empty list. The idea inbox reads ideas already on lists; its add-to-list action names a missing service route.Capture and memory have gapsProduct-link parsing has a helper but no connected creation route. History panels still say “coming soon.” Global search is also unfinished.Surprises need real protectionList privacy labels exist, but opening a list directly has no owner check. The promised recipient-safe hiding is not established.Customization is only half connectedThe options editor exists, while many forms still validate against fixed choices. Option usage is reported as empty rather than measured.
The core intentsGive every rooma clear purpose.The whole home: turn scattered ideas and shared mental load into thoughtful gifts and confident coordination, year-round.Family memoryRemember people, relationships, preferences, celebrations and spending across seasons.Shared serviceKeep changes consistent, calculate useful totals and help partners coordinate without double-buying.Browser tableMake coverage, choices, purchases and responsibilities understandable at a glance.Phone doorwayCapture an idea when it occurs and handle small decisions comfortably while out.Outside connectionsBring browsing and calendars closer to planning, and send timely reminders without duplicating effort.Private foundationsKeep household memory under family control and recover it when the host or app changes.
What to keepKeep the house.Refurnish the living space.Reuse the family model, useful service boundaries and existing pieces of the app. A wholesale restart would throw away substantial domain learning. The fresh-database break needs resolving before trusting family data to an upgrade. Later, reconsider the screens and phone experience around today’s native iPhone and web capabilities instead of resuming every old plan.Keep the memory and the craftPeople, occasions, linked gifts, budgets, comments and image handling are useful material. The shared web component library and current approved design language offer ingredients for a coherent family experience.Drop inherited obligationsRetire superseded designs, duplicate presentation patterns and blanket live-update complexity. Treat old plans as historical intentions. Track any chosen revival work explicitly in IntentTree.The current design estate includes web tokens and a family illustration canon. The Apple token bridge still has unresolved fit and verification gaps; it is not a ready-made native app kit. A family-first product can nourish shared capture, design and collaboration practices while keeping its own household purpose.This is a reuse recommendation. New mock-ups, product choices and implementation come after you read it.
Private local archaeology. Original app sources unchanged. Nothing committed, pushed or published. Everything started for this visit has been stopped.
